traits: Seed head with several finger-like branches spreading out from one point
Sprawling, low, star-shaped growth radiating outward from a central point
Coarser, lighter green blades than most surrounding turf
Stems root wherever they touch soil, thickening the patch over a season

look_alikes.difference: Crabgrass has a flat, star-shaped habit with a rounded stem; goosegrass has a flattened rosette with a whitish-silvery base and stiffer blades.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the base of the plant, checking for a white or silvery flattened crown.

look_alikes.difference: Crabgrass is a sprawling annual with finger-like seed branches and no rhizomes; bahiagrass is a perennial with a Y-shaped seed stalk and thick rhizomes.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the seed head shape and whether digging at the base reveals thick rhizomes.

copy.what_it_means: A common warm-season weed that moves into thin spots and spreads out fast once established, producing huge amounts of seed. A technician looks at how thin the turf is, the season, and coverage before recommending an approach, since a thicker lawn is the best long-term defense.
copy.fact: A single crabgrass plant can produce thousands of seeds in a season, which is why a few missed patches can turn into a lawn-wide problem the following year.
copy.blurb: A fast-spreading summer weed that fills in thin turf and produces huge amounts of seed.

tech_notes: Cold-sensitive annual — dies back with the first hard frost, but seed persists in the soil for the next season. Per label if herbicide is used.

id_cues: Seed head has several finger-like branches radiating from one point
Grows low and star-shaped, spreading out from a central point
Coarser, lighter green than the surrounding lawn
Stems root at the nodes wherever they touch soil

traits: Flattened, whitish-to-silvery crown at the base where the blades emerge, visible when parted
Coarse, stiff, dark green blades in a low, flattened rosette
Zipper-like seed head with two or more spikes joined near the tip
Common in compacted, wet, high-traffic areas like paths and driveway edges

look_alikes.difference: Goosegrass has a whitish-silvery flattened crown at the base and stiffer blades; crabgrass has a rounder stem, no silvery crown, a looser sprawling habit.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the base of the plant checking for a white or silvery flattened crown.

look_alikes.difference: Goosegrass has longer zipper spikes and a silvery flattened crown; crowfootgrass has short spikes with a bare tip, hairy margins, no silvery base.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up comparing the base (silvery crown or not) and the seed head shape (zipper vs. radiating spikes).

copy.what_it_means: A tough, compaction-loving weed that shows up most in high-traffic areas, along paths, and near driveway edges where soil is packed hard and stays wet. A technician looks at how compacted and thin the turf is, the season, and coverage before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Its silvery-white, flattened base is a dead giveaway once you know to look for it — few other lawn weeds have that same crown color right where the blades emerge from the ground.
copy.blurb: A tough weed that thrives in compacted, high-traffic soil along paths and driveway edges.

tech_notes: Compaction is the underlying driver — aeration alongside any treatment addresses the cause rather than just the symptom. Per label if herbicide is used.

id_cues: Flattened, whitish-to-silvery crown at the base, visible when the blades are parted
Coarse, stiff, dark green blades in a low, flattened rosette
Zipper-like seed head with two or more spikes joined near the tip
Found in compacted, wet spots — paths, driveway edges, high-traffic areas

traits: Stiff, sharply pointed rhizome tips (the "torpedo") that can pierce bare skin if handled
Coarser, more upright, grayish-green blades than surrounding St. Augustine or bahia
Deep, tough, wide-ranging rhizome network that can run many feet from the visible patch
Forms a distinct patch that stands out in texture and color from the lawn around it

look_alikes.difference: Torpedograss has coarser, grayish-green blades and hard, sharp rhizome tips; St. Augustine has wide, blunt blades on soft surface runners, no sharp points.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up comparing blade texture and color, plus a dug-up rhizome tip checked for a hard, sharp point; wear sturdy gloves, since the tip can pierce skin.

look_alikes.difference: Torpedograss has stiffer blades and sharply pointed rhizome tips that can pierce skin; bermudagrass has fine, soft blades and blunt, thin rhizomes throughout.
look_alikes.next_photo: Wearing sturdy gloves, a close-up of a dug-up rhizome tip — a hard, sharp point that can pierce skin (torpedograss) versus a blunt, thin rhizome (bermuda).

copy.what_it_means: One of the most invasive grasses in Florida, spreading on deep, tough rhizomes that run for many feet and are genuinely difficult to fully remove from a lawn. A technician evaluates the weed, turf type, season, and coverage to explain why this one needs a different, more patient approach than an ordinary grassy weed.
copy.fact: Its rhizomes are unusually tough and deep-running, which is part of why it's considered one of Florida's most invasive plants.
copy.blurb: An aggressive, deep-rhizomed grass that's genuinely hard to remove once it establishes in a lawn.

tech_notes: Deep rhizome network makes spot treatment unreliable; set expectations for a longer-term, staged approach rather than a single application. Per label if herbicide is used.

id_cues: Dig up a rhizome tip — hard, sharp, and torpedo-shaped, capable of piercing skin
Coarser, more upright, grayish-green blades than surrounding turf
Forms a visibly different-textured, different-colored patch in the lawn

traits: Flat, broadly linear, yellow-green leaf blades with rough margins and fine hairs
Stems lie flat with the tips turning upward, rooting at the nodes as they spread
Seed head has several angled, flag-like branches along a central stalk
Low, sprawling, creeping growth typical of a summer annual

look_alikes.difference: Alexandergrass has flat, hairy, yellow-green blades and flag-like seedhead branches; crabgrass has smoother blades and finger-like branches from one point.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the leaf surface (hairy vs. smoother) and the seed head branch pattern.

look_alikes.difference: Alexandergrass has broader, hairier, yellow-green blades; tropical signalgrass has narrower blades and low, mat-forming stems rooting densely at every node.
look_alikes.next_photo: Not reliably separable from a photo alone — a technician checks leaf hairiness and how densely the stems root along the ground.

copy.what_it_means: A summer annual grassy weed that favors moist, open ground and spreads by creeping, rooting stems. A technician looks at how thin the turf is, the season, and coverage before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Its seed head branches fan out at an angle like small signal flags, which is part of why it's sometimes confused with its close relative, signalgrass.
copy.blurb: A creeping summer annual grass that spreads through moist, open turf on rooting stems.

tech_notes: Closely related to tropical signalgrass; confirm which is present since management timing can differ. Per label if herbicide is used.

id_cues: Flat, yellow-green blades with rough, hairy margins
Stems lie flat, tips turning upward, rooting at the nodes

Grows in moist, open, sunny ground

traits: Seed head with three to five thick spikelets radiating from a single point — a true crow's-foot shape
Blades with fine, outward-pointing hairs along the margins
Stems bend and root at the lower nodes, with tips rising up to about two feet
Common in dry, sandy, disturbed soil and thin turf

look_alikes.difference: Crowfootgrass has short spikes with a bare tip and hairy leaf margins, no silvery base; goosegrass has longer zipper spikes and a silvery flattened crown.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up comparing the seed head (radiating spikes vs. zipper shape) and the base of the plant for a silvery crown.

look_alikes.difference: Crowfootgrass has thick, radiating spikelets and hairy leaf margins; crabgrass has thinner finger-like branches and a smoother, sprawling, star-shaped habit.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the seed head branch thickness and whether the leaf margins are noticeably hairy.

copy.what_it_means: A warm-season annual that favors dry, sandy, thin turf and disturbed soil, named for the crow's-foot shape of its seed head. A technician looks at how thin the turf is, the season, and coverage before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Its seed head really does look like a bird's foot, with three to five thick spikelets fanning out from a single point at the top of the stalk.
copy.blurb: A dry-soil summer weed named for its distinctive crow's-foot-shaped seed head.

tech_notes: Favors dry, sandy, thin turf; improving turf density is the underlying long-term fix. Per label if herbicide is used.

traits: Leaf margins with evenly spaced hairs running at least a third of the blade's length
Seed head is a slanted spike with two rows of seed along one side of the stem
Flowering stalks stay slanted even in a regularly mowed lawn
Tolerates close mowing better than many other grassy weeds

look_alikes.difference: Thin paspalum has evenly spaced leaf-margin hairs and one slanted seed spike; crabgrass has smoother margins and finger-like branches from one point.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the leaf margin for evenly spaced hairs and the seed head shape.

look_alikes.difference: Thin paspalum has a slanted, two-rowed seed spike and a low sprawling habit; smutgrass grows as a tight upright bunch, its seed head often blackened by fungus.
look_alikes.next_photo: A wide shot of the growth habit (sprawling vs. tight upright bunch) and a close-up of the seed head for black fungus.

copy.what_it_means: A grassy weed that can tolerate closer mowing than most others, which is part of why it can persist in well-kept lawns. A technician looks at coverage, turf type, and season before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Its flowering stalks stay slanted to one side even in a lawn that's mowed regularly, which is a helpful, easy tell once you know to look for it.
copy.blurb: A grassy weed that tolerates close mowing better than most, letting it persist in well-kept lawns.

tech_notes: Tolerates lower mowing heights than most grassy weeds, which can let it persist in otherwise well-maintained turf. Per label if herbicide is used.

review.notes: SWFL-specific range and seasonal peak are a best-estimate judgment call; the cited USDA NRCS fact sheet gives only a broad Atlantic/Gulf Coastal Plain range with no Florida county-level detail.

traits: Tight, upright bunch grass, roughly 8-10 inches across at the base

look_alikes.difference: Smutgrass grows as a tight upright bunch with a narrow, often black, fungus-coated seedhead; thin paspalum sprawls low with a slanted, two-rowed seed spike.
look_alikes.next_photo: A wide shot of the growth habit (tight bunch vs. sprawling) and a close-up of the seedhead for black fungus.

copy.what_it_means: A tough, tufted grass that forms distinct clumps and is genuinely difficult to control once established, since ordinary mowing barely slows it down. A technician evaluates coverage, turf type, and season to explain the different approach this one usually needs compared to an ordinary grassy weed.
copy.fact: Its seedhead is often coated in a black fungus, which is where the name "smutgrass" comes from.
copy.blurb: A tough, clump-forming grass with a telltale black, fungus-coated seedhead — genuinely hard to control once established.

tech_notes: Established clumps are notably persistent; set expectations for a staged approach and repeat monitoring rather than a single application. Per label if herbicide is used.

look_alikes.difference: Tropical signalgrass has narrow blades and low, densely rooting, mat-forming stems; alexandergrass has broader, hairier, yellow-green blades, a looser habit.
look_alikes.next_photo: Not reliably separable from a photo alone — a technician checks leaf hairiness and how densely the stems root along the ground.

look_alikes.difference: Tropical signalgrass has narrower blades and a small seed head with angled branches; St. Augustine has wide, blunt blades, no visible seed head when mowed.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of blade width and whether a small, branched seed head is present above the turf.

copy.what_it_means: A warm-season perennial grass that spreads on densely rooting stems, forming a thick mat that's hard to distinguish from turf until well established. A technician looks at how far it has spread, turf type, season, and coverage, since it's one of the more persistent grassy weeds in Florida lawns.
copy.fact: It roots so readily at the nodes that a single mowed-off fragment left on the lawn can start a brand-new patch elsewhere.
copy.blurb: A mat-forming grassy weed that spreads readily by rooting stems and can be hard to spot until well established.

tech_notes: One of the more persistent grassy weeds in FL turf per UF/IFAS EDIS ENH1132/EP393; field germination occurs once soil temperatures reach about 77°F and needs soil pH 5-6, which is common in Florida soils. Per label if herbicide is used; mower sanitation helps limit spread from fragments.
